paper.title: A Machine Learning Model for Predicting 28-Day Mortality in Critically Ill Ischemic Stroke Patients With Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome: A Retrospective Cohort Study Based on MIMIC-IV and eICU Databases.
paper.abstract:
Introduction: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) commonly complicates ischemic stroke (IS) in critically ill patients and is associated with increased mortality. We aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable model for predicting 28-day mortality in this population.
Methods: We used the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database for model development and internal validation and the eICU database for external validation. Critically ill IS patients with SIRS during the first ICU day were included. The model predicted mortality occurring between the 24-hour landmark and day 28 after ICU admission. MIMIC-IV patients were randomly divided into training and testing sets at a 7:3 ratio. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression selected predictors for six algorithms. The model with the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in the testing set was externally validated and compared with the Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score (OASIS) alone. Performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis.
Results: The study included 2,438 patients: 1,620 from MIMIC-IV and 818 from eICU. Nine predictors were selected: age, white blood cell count, red blood cell distribution width, blood urea nitrogen, anion gap, Charlson Comorbidity Index, SIRS score, OASIS, and mechanical ventilation. Among the six models evaluated in the testing set, logistic regression (LR) achieved the highest AUC (0.846) and was therefore selected for external validation. In the external validation cohort, the LR model achieved a higher AUC than OASIS alone (0.794 vs. 0.758), and showed reasonable calibration and potential clinical utility.
Conclusion: We developed and externally validated an interpretable ML-based model for predicting 28-day mortality in critically ill IS patients with SIRS. The LR model showed good discrimination and reasonable calibration in external validation. Prospective multicenter validation and clinical-impact assessment are required before implementation.

paper.title: Machine learning-based differentiation of malignant and non-malignant pleural effusion in lung cancer patients: a multicenter retrospective study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Malignant pleural effusion (MPE) is a common complication of lung cancer and is associated with poor prognosis and substantial clinical burden. Differentiating malignant from non-malignant pleural effusion remains challenging, particularly when definitive pleural fluid cytology or pleural biopsy results are pending, inconclusive, or delayed. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning-based model for auxiliary classification of MPE in lung cancer patients after lung cancer diagnosis and partial tumor-related pathological or staging information had been obtained.
Methods: In this retrospective multicenter study, a total of 715 lung cancer patients with pleural effusion were included from two tertiary hospitals. The Shanxi cohort from Heping Hospital Affiliated to Changzhi Medical College included 420 patients and was used as the development cohort, whereas the Anhui cohort from Tongling People's Hospital included 295 patients and served as the independent external validation cohort. The development cohort was randomly divided into a training set and an internal test set at a ratio of 7:3, resulting in 295 patients in the training set and 125 patients in the internal test set. Clinical, laboratory, and pathological variables were collected. Feature selection was performed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression within the training set. Seven machine-learning algorithms were developed and evaluated. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration analysis, and decision curve analysis. External validation was conducted using the independent Anhui cohort.
Results: Six predictors were selected, including age, Ki-67 index, lymph node metastasis, tumor size, total cholesterol, and serum albumin. Multiple machine learning models demonstrated comparable performance in internal validation. The XGBoost model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.97 in the internal test set and 0.91 in the independent external validation cohort. At the training-derived operating threshold, the external validation sensitivity was 0.35 and the specificity was 0.98, indicating favorable overall discrimination but limited rule-out performance. SHAP analysis suggested that tumor burden-related variables and systemic condition had substantial influence on model output.
Conclusion: A machine learning-based model was developed for auxiliary classification of malignant and non-malignant pleural effusion in lung cancer patients after lung cancer diagnosis and partial tumor-related pathological or staging information had been obtained. The model showed favorable discrimination but limited sensitivity at the training-derived operating threshold in external validation and should therefore be regarded only as a candidate auxiliary tool. Further prospective and multicenter validation and recalibration are required before clinical implementation, and the model is not intended to replace cytological or histopathological confirmation.

paper.title: Decision system for combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma distant metastasis: a retrospective cohort study based on machine learning.
paper.abstract:
Background: Combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma (CHC) is a rare primary liver cancer with low incidence and poor prognosis. CHC can develop distant metastasis (DM) at an early stage, which severely shortens the survival time of patients. We aimed to use machine learning (ML) to construct a decision-making system to assess risk factors for the development of DM in CHC patients.
Methods: 1180 CHC patients from the SEER database between 2000 and 2020 were collected and randomized into the train set and internal test group in a 7:3 ratio. Patients diagnosed with CHC at our hospital between 2011 and 2018 were also collected as the external validation set (N = 125). Patients with CHC were divided into a metastasis group and a non-metastasis group according to the occurrence of DM. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to evaluate the risk factors influencing DM of CHC patients in the training set. We screened the feature variables based on random forest (RF) and forward feature importance sequences. Then we incorporated them into six ML algorithms for constructing machine learning models and used 10-fold cross-validation for internal validation. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, precision-recall curve (PRC), calibration curve (CC), and confusion Matrix (CM) were used to evaluate the predictive ability of the models. We determined the importance ranking of risk factors for DM in CHC patients using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and further used SHAP to analyze the interpretability of the black-box model. Finally, we built a web risk calculator based on the optimal performance model to facilitate its clinical application.
Results: A total of six variables were selected for constructing the decision model. Extreme gradient boosting (XGB) obtained the most significant recognition ability, with ROCAUC = 0.863, accuracy of 0.802, sensitivity of 0.875, and PRAUC of 0.642 in the internal test set. 10-fold cross-validation results showed that the ROCAUC of XGB was 0.989, with a standard error of 0.019. The SHAP method revealed that node, surgery, age, grade, primary site, and race are the top 6 key variables that contribute to the occurrence of DM in CHC. In addition, the analysis of two typical cases proved the reliability of the model.
Conclusions: The XGB model outperforms other machine learning methods in recognizing the occurrence of distant metastases in CHC patients, and has a high degree of utility and reliability to inform clinical treatment decisions for patients.

paper.title: Prediction of Postoperative Neurological Function Recovery in Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy Using MRI-based Delta-Radiomics Combined with Interpretable Machine Learning Model.
paper.abstract: Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy (CSM) presents progressive neurological deterioration and highly variable postoperative outcomes, while existing prognostic assessment methods have inherent limitations. This dual-center study developed an interpretable MRI-based delta-radiomics model for individualized CSM postoperative prognosis evaluation. A total of 237 CSM patients from Center 1 and 96 patients from Center 2 who underwent decompression surgery were retrospectively enrolled. The Center 1 cohort was stratified by clinical outcomes and randomly divided into training (n = 165) and internal testing (n = 72) cohorts at a 7:3 ratio, while the Center 2 cohort served as an independent external validation set (n = 96). Radiomic features were extracted from pre- and postoperative T2WI MRI images, and delta-radiomic features were calculated. LASSO regression and spearman correlation analysis were applied to screen core radiomic features, and clinical-routine imaging features. Three prediction models were constructed via five machine learning algorithms. Model performance was evaluated using AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score, and pairwise comparisons performed via the DeLong and McNemar tests. Calibration curves and radar charts were generated to determine the optimal algorithm for each model. Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis were performed to assess clinical benefit and model interpretability. Baseline data were well balanced. 16 preoperative radiomic features, 15 delta-radiomic features, and 5 clinical-routine imaging features were finally selected. The XGBoost-based delta-radiomic model achieved the highest numerical AUCs in the internal test (0.899) and external validation (0.802) sets, demonstrating a statistically significant improvement in AUC compared to both the preoperative radiomic model and the clinical-routine imaging model. The model maintained a balanced performance profile across cohorts. This model maintained a higher clinical net benefit across wide threshold ranges. SHAP analysis identified wavelet-domain texture features as risk factors for poor prognosis, while gradient-domain kurtosis features showed bidirectional regulatory effects. Overall, the MRI-based delta-radiomic model effectively predicts long-term neurological recovery in CSM patients. The delta-radiomic model exhibits a more balanced performance profile and statistically better generalizability. By utilizing routine short-term postoperative MRI (within 7 days), this interpretable model holds promise as an objective tool for early prediction of 12-month postoperative neurological recovery.

paper.title: Early Prehospital Prediction of Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Derivation and External Validation of the MIRA-29 Score.
paper.abstract:
Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac (OHCA) arrest is a frequent emergency, and few patients will survive with good neurological outcome. Identification of patients with a low likelihood of meaningful recovery represents a major clinical challenge. Numerous scores have been developed to guide decision-making after OHCA, with variable goals and targets, but most of them have been validated on small cohorts, integrates variables not available in the prehospital field, or do have low prediction values. MIRA-29 score aimed to only rely on simple clinical variables, available in the prehospital setting. We hypothetized that such score will provide incremental neurological prognosis value at an early-stage following OHCA.
Methods: MIRA-29 score was derived and internally validated over a five-year period on a prospective cohort of 1099 adult patients, including all OHCA treated by our territory dispatch center. Multivariate analysis identified independent variables within the database, that were used to optimize the prediction model using machine-learning and genetic algorithms. The score was subsequently validated externally on 82 696 patients extracted from the French national cardiac arrest registry (RéAC).
Results: Out from the 1099 patients, 85 patients (7.7%) had a favorable neurological outcome. Multivariate analysis identified five independent variables associated with neurological outcome: age, low-flow duration, number of external electric shock, epinephrine dose, and the OHCA site (street, public facility, home). After model optimization and machine-learning, age was not retained within the final model. External validation depicted a precision of 0.86 and a recall of 0.88 of the model. The F1-Score and accuracy are respectively 0.87 and 0.88, and specificity for a bad neurological prognosis is 0.99.
Conclusion: MIRA‑29 strength lies on its ability to reliably identify patients with extremely high probability of poor neurological outcome, while being based on four simple clinical variables. The prospective validation of MIRA-29 in the clinical setting may evaluate its impact on clinical decision making.

paper.title: Ultrasound deep learning for predicting aggressiveness in papillary thyroid carcinoma: an exploratory analysis of transcriptomic correlates.
paper.abstract:
Background: Preoperative assessment of aggressiveness in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is important for individualized treatment decision-making. This study aimed to develop a deep learning (DL) model to predict PTC aggressiveness and, in an exploratory analysis, to assess associations between model-derived imaging phenotypes and transcriptomic pathway signatures.
Methods: Preoperative ultrasound images from 1023 patients with PTC were used to develop a DL model for aggressiveness prediction, and clinical features were further integrated to construct a combined DL-Clinic model. Grad-CAM was applied to generate class-specific heatmaps, and mean Grad-CAM activation intensities were extracted from the whole lesion ROI and its core, marginal, and microcalcification regions. Patients were further stratified according to the DL score and regional activation intensity, followed by exploratory GSEA to assess transcriptomic pathway associations.
Results: The DL-Clinic model improved the AUCs to 0.834, 0.759, and 0.750 in the internal validation, external test, and prospective test sets, respectively. Multivariable analysis identified the DL score as the strongest independent predictor of PTC aggressiveness (OR = 3.498, p < 0.001). Grad-CAM analysis showed higher activation intensity in the ROI and all subregions of aggressive cases. Exploratory GSEA suggested that high-risk and high-activation phenotypes tended to be associated with enrichment of pathways related to tumor proliferation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and antigen processing, whereas low-risk and low-activation phenotypes were predominantly enriched in immune-related pathways.
Conclusion: The DL-Clinic model demonstrated discriminatory performance for the preoperative prediction of PTC aggressiveness. Exploratory imaging-transcriptomic analyses suggested associations between model-derived imaging phenotypes and transcriptomic pathway signatures. Further prospective multicenter studies are needed to establish the model's clinical utility, and these exploratory imaging-transcriptomic associations require independent validation.

paper.title: An early prediction model for MODS in patients with traumatic sepsis: a development and external validation study.
paper.abstract: Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS) is a severe complication of traumatic sepsis and is associated with high mortality and healthcare costs. Early risk stratification is critical, but clinically validated tools for predicting MODS in traumatic sepsis are lacking. We developed and validated a machine learning model for early MODS prediction in patients with traumatic sepsis. We enrolled 650 ICU patients with traumatic sepsis: 338 from a tertiary hospital ICU (development cohort; randomly divided into training and internal validation sets at 8:2) and 312 from MIMIC-IV (external validation cohort). Logistic regression, decision tree, extreme gradient boosting machine, neural network, random forest, and LightGBM were trained using independent risk factors identified by multivariable logistic regression. The development cohort MODS incidence was 38.46% (130/338). Seven independent risk factors were identified: age, open trauma, Injury Severity Score, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), procalcitonin, D-dimer, and serum creatinine. In internal validation, random forest achieved the highest AUC (0.933, 95% CI: 0.905‒0.961), followed by LightGBM (0.911, 95% CI: 0.879‒0.943) and extreme gradient boosting (0.910, 95% CI: 0.878‒0.942). In external validation, LightGBM achieved the highest AUC (0.751, 95% CI: 0.698‒0.804), followed by extreme gradient boosting (0.748, 95% CI: 0.695‒0.801) and neural network (0.739, 95% CI: 0.685‒0.793). A composite score integrating AUCs, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score, Brier score, and log loss ranked LightGBM first (score 92), making it the optimal model for early MODS risk prediction in this patient population.

paper.title: Structural MRI Morphometry Across the Alzheimer's Disease Spectrum: Classification and Generalization.
paper.abstract: Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides quantitative measures of brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but reliable classification also depends on the evaluation protocol and performance across cohorts. This study assessed a morphometry-based approach for distinguishing cognitively normal (CN) participants, those with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and those with AD. The primary cohort included 815 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), with one screening MRI per participant and predefined training, validation, and test sets. MRI records were linked to FreeSurfer measurements using exact participant and image identifiers. A multinomial L2-regularized logistic regression classifier used 42 predefined structural features and five-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition site. In the held-out three-class test (n = 121), balanced accuracy was 0.6119 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.5291-0.6873) and the macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) was 0.7525. Recall was 0.8529 for CN, 0.2931 for MCI, and 0.6897 for AD. Additional development analyses examined demographic and clinical variables separately from the primary MRI-only result. For the binary transfer experiment, a separate ADNI-trained CN-versus-AD model using 32 shared morphometric features achieved balanced accuracy of 0.8458 and ROC-AUC of 0.9016 in site-grouped out-of-fold evaluation. The fixed model was then tested without target-cohort tuning on 181 older participants from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-1), grouped by Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR = 0 versus CDR > 0). External balanced accuracy was 0.6492 (95% CI: 0.5799-0.7158) and ROC-AUC was 0.7502. Because ADNI diagnoses and OASIS-1 CDR groups are not identical clinical endpoints, the external experiment was interpreted separately from the primary three-class analysis. The results demonstrate the value of reporting class-specific performance and independent-cohort evaluation when assessing structural MRI morphometry.

paper.title: Identification of Proteomic Subtypes with Differential Responses to Immune Checkpoint Inhibition in Cutaneous Melanoma.
paper.abstract:
Purpose: Predictive biomarkers for combined PD-1/CTLA-4 blockade in metastatic melanoma remain limited. We analyzed pretreatment proteogenomic data to define response and resistance biology.
Experimental Design: We profiled 208 pretreatment FFPE specimens from patients with metastatic cutaneous melanoma treated across 12 institutions, including 164 receiving dual PD-1+CTLA-4 blockade (Discovery, n=97; Validation 1, n=67) and 44 receiving PD-1 monotherapy. Tumors underwent TMT-based proteomics, RNA sequencing, and targeted/low-pass whole-genome sequencing. Pathway clustering, survival modeling, deconvolution, and machine-learning classification defined and validated subtype signatures.
Results: Proteomic pathway clustering identified three reproducible ICI subtypes: immune-enriched ICI-sensitive, ribosome-high, and EMT-like/stromal-enriched. Subtypes stratified progression-free survival after dual ICI in the Discovery (P=0.01) and Validation 1 cohorts (P=0.02). The ICI-sensitive subtype had the highest responder fraction (74% and 73%), compared with ribosome-high (67% and 60%) and EMT-like tumors (44% and 43%) in the Discovery and Validation 1 cohorts, respectively. Subtype-outcome associations were consistent with previous immunotherapy datasets, with pooled hazard ratios ≈0.5-0.8 for immune-enriched tumors. Subtypes plus clinical variables predicted 3-year progression/death better than clinical variables alone in Validation 1 (AUC 0.80 vs 0.64). A 127-protein classifier recapitulated subtype membership in Validation 1 (AUC 0.89-0.97) and predicted 3-year progression/death with AUC 0.79. Subtypes reflected distinct immune, translational, and stromal/ECM programs and nominated POLR3A-associated biology as a candidate resistance axis.
Conclusions: Proteomic pathway states define reproducible, biologically interpretable melanoma subtypes associated with differential benefit from dual PD-1/CTLA-4 blockade. A clinically tractable 127-protein classifier provides a foundation for prospective biomarker-driven combination immunotherapy trials.

paper.title: Assessment of Distributive DNA Methylation Profiling for Central Nervous System Tumor Classification Between Laboratories in the United States and Brazil.
paper.abstract:
Context.—: Implementation of machine learning-based central nervous system (CNS) tumor classifiers remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where many centers lack the infrastructure, expertise, or financial resources required for clinical deployment. Distributive testing offers a practical pathway for broader adoption, allowing centers without in-house capabilities to access validated classification pipelines. Understanding sample and data quality and classifier performance in the local patient population is a critical initial step in determining the feasibility of this approach.
Objective.—: To evaluate whether methylation data generated in a Brazilian site could support tumor classification, using a US-based clinical-grade methylation classifier.
Design.—: We conducted retrospective and prospective analyses of preanalytic parameters, methylation testing quality metrics, and classifier outputs on data generated in Brazil. Quality metric distributions from study samples were compared with in-house clinical data. Classifier performance was assessed by reviewing concordance with histopathology and available ancillary testing information.
Results.—: A total of 151 unique CNS tumor samples, representing major tumor families, were evaluated. Preanalytic metrics of the study samples were comparable to those from the US-based laboratory. Some differences in methylation testing metrics reflected instrumentation variation. Confident classifications matching histologic diagnosis were achieved in 141 of 151 samples (93.4%), with ancillary testing and quality control data supporting the classifier call in 6 additional cases. Classifier-histopathology concordance showed no significant correlation with preanalytic or methylation metrics.
Conclusions.—: Samples processed in Brazil met US-comparable quality standards, supporting robust classifier performance and feasibility of distributive methylation testing.

paper.title: Machine learning assisted thermal reperfusion mapping reveals real-time changes in foot microcirculation during endovascular revascularisation.
paper.abstract:
Objective: To test the feasibility of a novel thermal perfusion imaging and mapping system to show microcirculatory changes of plantar foot angiosomes during endovascular procedures.
Methods: A prospective, exploratory MedTech development study was designed to test the system in a series of patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI). Intraprocedural video thermography was performed using a 320 × 240 pixel resolution, thermal camera. Initial analysis was manual, re- positioning regions of interest (ROIs) within each of five plantar foot angiosomes. Subsequent automation using deep learning segmentation allowed ROI tracking from initial frame to procedure end. Isotherms (thermal contours) created and applied to the segmented surface provide quantitative, real-time changes in the percentage distribution of isotherms overlying both treated and contralateral foot angiosomes during the procedure.
Results: Of 23 participants recruited, video thermography was obtained in 21 patients admitted with moderate-severe disease complexity; femoral-popliteal segment only (n = 13), femoral-popliteal and infrapopliteal disease (n = 5) and infrapopliteal disease only (n = 3). Changes in percentage distribution of each isotherm overlay revealed two broad groups; plantar foot thermal perfusion responders (n = 12) and non-responders (n = 9). In responders, revascularisation led to a series of 'dynamic' phases where temperature increased in one, or more, angiosomes; 'hottest' isotherms expanded significantly (p = .002) in response to endovascular procedures. In thermal perfusion non-responders, no significant change in isotherm percentage distribution was observed.
Conclusion: Thermal perfusion imaging is feasible using the novel implemented deep learning system. Clinicians can gain insight about microcirculatory changes at foot angiosomes in response to treatment based on three parameters; (i) temporal temperature profiles of each angiosome, (ii) real-time changes in the percentage distribution of isotherms across the plantar surface during the intervention, (iii) angiosome-specific cutaneous perfusion responses to balloon inflation and/or stent deployment. For patients with diabetes, locating the site of improved skin reperfusion has potential to predict treatment success for healing outcomes at the ulcer/woundosome.
